> 兌。亨，利貞。

Hexagram 58 is about pleasure, and its structure is unusually visible: five lines carry the character, and the one that does not is the one in danger.

## 兌: three senses that must stay apart

說文: 兌，說也 — 說, that is 悅, delight.

The shape is 儿 (a person) with 㕣; one account has it as a mouth opening and breath coming out.

So: the original sense is delight; the trigram's image is 澤, a marsh; and 兌 separately means "sharp," the point of a thing.

Three senses, kept apart. The chapter is about the first, and the second is what the shape of the hexagram supplies — two marshes, water over water.

## Five lines carry 兌, one does not

初九 和兌 — delight in harmony.
九二 孚兌 — delight with trust.
六三 來兌 — delight that comes to you.
九四 商兌 — delight weighed on a scale.
上六 引兌 — delight pulled toward you.

And 九五: 孚于剝，有厲 — trust in what is being stripped away.

Five lines with the same character attached is very rare in sixty-four hexagrams. And the verse that omits it is the one in the ruler's seat.

Which is the chapter's structure in one observation: all the ways of taking pleasure are named, and the position that could have the most of it is the position where the pleasure is not the subject at all — the subject is what it is trusting.

## 和兌 and 孚兌

和: harmony — delight that does not require anything of the other.
孚: trust — delight that has something underneath it.

Two opening lines, two conditions, both 吉. The hexagram does not start by warning. It starts by naming the two forms that are sound.

## 來兌 and 引兌

來兌: delight that arrives, that is brought to you. 凶.

引兌: delight that is drawn out, pulled toward oneself. The top line, with no verdict given.

So the hexagram distinguishes three directions: delight that is mutual (和), delight that is trusted (孚), and delight that comes toward you or is pulled toward you. The first two are the subject. The second two are the failure: pleasure as something received.

## 商兌

商: to measure, to reckon (商，度也).

商兌，未寧 — weighing the pleasure and not yet settled.

介疾有喜 — and this is the line where a character has to be rescued: 介 is not "great." 介 means a boundary, a dividing line (說文 介，畫也), extended to separation.

So 介疾 is drawing a line and putting the illness outside it. Read 介 as "great," and the whole line collapses into nonsense.

The fourth line's situation: the pleasure is still being weighed, nothing is settled, and the way through is to draw one boundary and keep the disease on the other side of it. Then there is 喜.

## 剝

剝: to strip, to peel away (說文 剝，裂也).

In this hexagram 剝 is yin stripping yang: the top yielding line outside, peeling layer after layer off the firm line in the ruler's seat.

孚于剝 — trusting the thing that is peeling you. 有厲.

Which is the exact danger of pleasure at the top: not excess. Trust placed in what is taking from you.

## The test

Take a pleasure you have — a habit, an arrangement, a way of being liked. Ask which of the five it is: 和 (mutual), 孚 (trusted), 來 (brought to you), 商 (still being weighed), 引 (pulled toward you). The hexagram gives a verdict for four of them, and the fifth it leaves blank.
